rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prominent Makkans wanted to join the Prophet’s teaching circle but disliked association with lower-status followers and asked him to send them away.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed when a group of prominent Makkans indicated that they wished to join the Prophet’s teaching circle

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some reports say the Makkans asked only that the poor followers be moved to the back rows of prayer, not expelled altogether.
rows.anchor: Some reports indicate the Prophet was not asked to send away these followers altogether, but rather to send them to the back rows of prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet refused to drive away his poorer followers, as Noah refused similar demands, though he was prepared to have them depart temporarily when prominent Makkans visited.
rows.anchor: The Prophet refused to “drive away” his poorer followers (in 11:27–29 and 26:111–14 Noah refuses to do the same)

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ, W
rows.claim: The verse was revealed to forbid the Prophet from driving away his pious followers who worship morning and evening.
rows.anchor: This verse was then revealed forbidding him from “driving away” his pious followers who call upon their Lord morning and evening (IK, R, Ṭ, W)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, W
rows.claim: Quran 18:28 is linked to a similar circumstance and is reportedly a revelation about that situation.
rows.anchor: reportedly revealed in a similar circumstance (Ṭ, W)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 80:1–10 recounts the incident in which the Prophet is admonished for showing displeasure when a poor blind man came instead of wealthier Makkans.
rows.anchor: about the incident in which the Prophet is admonished for registering displeasure when his teaching attracted a poor blind man rather than the wealthier Makkans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These passages raise the question of how the Prophet could appear to favor status-conscious Makkans over sincere followers, given that driving them away would make him a wrongdoer.
rows.anchor: These passages raise the question of how the Prophet could seem to favor these prominent Makkans

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the Prophet’s possible initial willingness to accommodate the Makkans was intended only to facilitate their acceptance of Islam.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī argues that even if the Prophet were initially prepared to accede to the Makkans’ demand

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reasons that the poor followers could be instructed another time, so no spiritual harm would come to them.
rows.anchor: his intention was only to facilitate their acceptance of Islam, and since the Prophet could continue to instruct his poorer followers at another time

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī holds that the Prophet did not sin by initially appearing willing to accommodate the demand because his intention was good.
rows.anchor: cannot be said to have sinned in his apparent initial willingness to accommodate the Makkans’ demand (R)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Morning and evening invocation may mean the five canonical prayers performed at their appointed times.
rows.anchor: refer to praying the five canonical prayers at their prescribed times

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Morning and evening invocation may mean supererogatory remembrance of God or Quran recitation.
rows.anchor: performing supererogatory acts of invoking God

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The invocation may include all these practices together.
rows.anchor: or to all of them (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Desiring God’s Face can mean literally hoping to see it, as a sincere lover longs to see the beloved’s face.
rows.anchor: with the hope of seeing God’s Face, for any sincere lover longs to see the face of the beloved (R)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Desiring God’s Face can also metaphorically mean sincerity of intention among the Prophet’s followers.
rows.anchor: it refers metaphorically to sincerity of intention among the Prophet’s followers (IK, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes the Quranic principle that no person bears another’s burden.
rows.anchor: echoes the Quranic idea that none shall bear the burden of another (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Syntactically, “their reckoning” most likely refers to the pious worshippers’ own reckoning, so the Prophet judges piety by outward acts.
rows.anchor: that the Prophet need only judge his followers’ piety on the basis of their outward actions (Z)

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say the verse responds to a Quraysh accusation that the poor followed the Prophet for material support rather than religious sincerity.
rows.anchor: Some commentators explain this as a response to an accusation made by some of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: On that reading, the Prophet need not assess possible ulterior motives behind his followers’ apparent piety.
rows.anchor: the verse was meant to indicate that the Prophet had no responsibility to assess the possible ulterior motives behind his

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: More plausibly, the reckoning concerns the prominent Makkans; the Prophet need not court their conversion by yielding to their demand to dismiss sincere followers.
rows.anchor: their embracing Islam that he should accede to their demand and “drive away”his pious followers at their behest (Z)
